title: Absurd to call someone ignorant of what he knows by sense, proof, or common fame
source_text: LIV. Sed absurde omnino, & contra rationem dicitur aliquis hoc vel illud nescire, & de eo incertus esse, propterea quod de eo fide divina certus non est: Nam sic dici possemus illa ipsa nescire, ac de iis incerti esse, quae demonstratione tenemus, sicut, terram esse sole minorem, aut quae percipimus sensu, ut saccharum esse dulce; vel quae testatur fama constans, ut Romanos olim hisce provinciis imperasse, & Homerum atque Virgilium fuisse Poetas insignes, quoniam de nullo istorum fide divina nos certos reddit. Quis tamen ferat dicentem quod ista incerta sint, aut quod aliquid horum, & similium, a peritis & doctis ignoretur atque nesciatur?
pass_a_gloss: But it is said altogether absurdly and against reason that someone does not know this or that, and is uncertain of it, because he is not certain of it by divine faith: For thus we could be said not to know those very things, and to be uncertain of them, which we hold by demonstration—as that the earth is smaller than the sun—or which we perceive by sense, as that sugar is sweet; or which constant fame testifies, as that the Romans once ruled these provinces, and that Homer and Virgil were distinguished poets, since divine faith makes us certain of none of those. Yet who would bear someone saying that those things are uncertain, or that something of these and the like is ignored and unknown by the skilled and learned?
pass_b_english: Lack of divine-faith certainty does not license the word ‘ignorance.’
Demonstration, sense, and common fame still yield knowledge in ordinary speech.
